## The idea

Given a network whose arcs have **lengths** (distances, travel times, costs), find the
shortest route from a source $s$ to a target $t$. It is the problem a navigation app
solves, and it appears inside many larger algorithms.

In the toy network below, the shortest route from $s$ to $t$ is
$s \to a \to d \to c \to t$, with length $2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 8$. The tempting direct-looking
routes are longer: $s \to a \to c \to t$ has length $10$.

## Dijkstra's algorithm

@dijkstra1959 gave the method still used today when all lengths are nonnegative. It
grows a set of nodes whose distance is **known for sure**:

1. Give $s$ the label $0$ and every other node the label $\infty$.
2. Among the nodes not yet final, pick one with the **smallest label** and make it final.
3. For each arc $(u, v)$ leaving that node $u$, if $\text{label}(u) + \ell_{uv} < \text{label}(v)$,
   lower $v$'s label to that value (and remember $u$ as $v$'s predecessor).
4. Repeat until $t$ (or every node) is final.

::: {#cell-fig-dijkstra .cell execution_count=3}

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (Dijkstra)
If all arc lengths are nonnegative, the label of each node is its true distance from
$s$ at the moment the node is made final. With a good priority queue the algorithm runs
in near-linear time in the number of arcs.
:::

The reason: when $u$ is picked, every other path to $u$ must leave the final set somewhere
and pay at least the label of a non-final node, which is already at least $u$'s label.
With a **negative** length, that argument fails: a path could come back cheaper later.

## Negative lengths: Bellman–Ford

When some lengths are negative (for example, arcs that represent profits), use the
**Bellman–Ford** method, due independently to @ford1956 and @bellman1958: repeat
"for every arc $(u, v)$, set $\text{label}(v) \leftarrow \min\{\text{label}(v),\ \text{label}(u) + \ell_{uv}\}$"
for $n - 1$ rounds, where $n$ is the number of nodes. If a further round still lowers
some label, the network contains a **negative cycle**, and shortest paths are not defined
(going round the cycle again always helps).

## The math

### The optimality equations

Let $d(v)$ be the distance from $s$ to $v$. If there is no negative cycle, the distances
are characterized by
$$
d(s) = 0, \qquad d(v) = \min_{(u, v)} \big( d(u) + \ell_{uv} \big) \quad (v \ne s).
$$
Equivalently, every part of a shortest path is itself a shortest path. These are the
equations of dynamic programming in their simplest form, and @bellman1958 solved the
routing problem exactly this way.

### Shortest paths as an LP, and distances as dual variables

Sending one unit of flow from $s$ to $t$ at minimum total length is an LP. With $x_{uv}$
the flow on arc $(u, v)$:
$$
\min \sum_{(u,v)} \ell_{uv} x_{uv}
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
\sum_{v} x_{uv} - \sum_{v} x_{vu} =
\begin{cases} 1 & u = s\\ -1 & u = t\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases},
\qquad x \ge 0 .
$$
Its [dual](../../linear-programming/duality/lp-duality.qmd) has one variable $\pi_v$ per
node, a **potential**:
$$
\max\ \pi_t - \pi_s \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \pi_v - \pi_u \le \ell_{uv} \ \text{ for every arc } (u, v).
$$

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (distances are optimal potentials)
If the network has no negative cycle and $t$ is reachable from $s$, the length of a
shortest $s$–$t$ path equals the maximum of $\pi_t - \pi_s$ over feasible potentials.
The distances $\pi_v = d(v)$ are an optimal potential, and an arc lies on a shortest path
exactly when it is **tight**: $d(v) - d(u) = \ell_{uv}$.
:::

Picture the potentials as heights, and each arc as a string of length $\ell_{uv}$ that
stops $v$ from rising more than $\ell_{uv}$ above $u$. Pull $t$ up as far as the strings
allow: the strings that go taut are the shortest path. In the toy network, every arc
satisfies $d(v) - d(u) \le \ell_{uv}$, and the four arcs of $s \to a \to d \to c \to t$ are
tight, adding up to $8 = d(t) - d(s)$.

## Why it works

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch: distances are optimal potentials
**Feasible.** For any arc $(u, v)$, going to $u$ by a shortest path and then along
$(u, v)$ is a path to $v$, so $d(v) \le d(u) + \ell_{uv}$.

**Weak duality.** For any $s$–$t$ path $P$ and feasible potentials,
$\ell(P) = \sum_{(u,v) \in P} \ell_{uv} \ge \sum_{(u,v) \in P} (\pi_v - \pi_u) = \pi_t - \pi_s$,
because the sum telescopes.

**Equality.** On a shortest path every arc is tight for $\pi = d$, so the inequality
holds with equality: $\ell(P) = d(t) - d(s)$. That is
[complementary slackness](../../linear-programming/duality/lp-duality.qmd).
:::

## In practice

- **Road routing** uses Dijkstra's algorithm plus heavy preprocessing and good guesses of
  the remaining distance, which is why maps answer in milliseconds on continental networks.
- **As a subproblem.** Shortest paths (often with extra resource constraints) are the
  pricing problem in column generation for vehicle routing and crew scheduling; see
  [Dantzig–Wolfe](../../decomposition-methods/dantzig-wolfe/theory-and-mechanism.qmd).
- **Project scheduling.** The earliest finish time of a project whose tasks must wait
  for each other is a *longest* path in an acyclic network, solved by the same equations
  in topological order.
